dialogue.shona: Mota yafa parwendo saka tiri kutsvaga rubatsiro.
dialogue.english: The car broke down on the trip, so we are looking for help.
dialogue.literal_gloss: Mota [car] • yafa [yafa] • parwendo [on / at rwendo] • saka [so / therefore] • tiri [tiri] • kutsvaga [to / at tsvaga] • rubatsiro [rubatsiro]

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('yafa')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'yafa' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Actions Happening Right Now: The '-ri ku-' Progressive
grammar_notes.content: To describe an action that is happening right now ('I am doing', 'it is raining', 'they are walking'), Shona uses the helper verb '-ri' ('am/is/are') followed by 'ku-' ('to') and the action verb. For people, the forms are 'ndiri ku-' (I am), 'uri ku-' (you are), 'ari ku-' (he/she is), 'tiri ku-' (we are), and 'vari ku-' (they are). In fast speech or writing, the two words are sometimes joined together (e.g., 'ndiri kuenda' or 'ndirikuenda').
grammar_notes.rule: [Subject + -ri] + ku-[verb] -> Ndiri kuverenga (I am reading) | Vari kufamba (They are walking) | Mvura iri kunaya (It is raining)

grammar_notes.title: Infinitive Verbs & Action Nouns with 'ku-' ('kutsvaga')
grammar_notes.content: Look at 'kutsvaga' in this sentence. Every Shona verb in its dictionary ('to do') form begins with 'ku-': for example, 'kudya' (to eat), 'kutenga' (to buy), 'kubhadhara' (to pay), 'kuona' (to see), and 'kurwa' (to fight). Because 'ku-' verbs also behave as action nouns ('eating', 'paying', 'working'), you can attach linking prefixes directly to them: 'yekubhadhara' ('for paying'), 'pakubikwa' ('in the cooking'), and 'nekuona' ('by/with seeing').
grammar_notes.rule: ku- + Verb Stem = 'to [verb] / [verb]-ing' (ku- + -tenga = kutenga, 'to buy'; ye- + kubhadhara = yekubhadhara, 'for paying')

cultural_notes.title: Roadside Solidarity ('Kutsvaga Rubatsiro') When a Vehicle Breaks Down
cultural_notes.content: Note how Shona idioms say a broken-down car has 'died' ('mota yafa')! Along Zimbabwean highways, fellow motorists and local villagers readily stop to offer tools, water, or mechanical help ('rubatsiro') to stranded travellers.

active_exercises.prompt: How do you say 'Our journey was very good' in Shona?
active_exercises.explanation: 'Rwendo rwedu' = 'Our journey' (taking 'rw-' agreement), 'rwakanga rwakanaka kwazvo' = 'was very good'.
